about: The roots of fish genus names, as a memory aid (Pierre, 2026-11-14, Q124 d: 'Je suis tes recommandations pour tout'), read from The ETYFish Project (etyfish.org), C. Scharpf: genera, by genus name: page, the slug of its ETYFish page (https://etyfish.org/<page>/); ety, the start of its entry there, verbatim; p, the parts that spell the name: [form] an ending or a part ETYFish does not gloss, [form, meaning, word] a meaning and its word, both verbatim in ety (word '' when the entry gives none), [form, genus, '', 'genus'] another genus the entry names, [form, person, '', 'honours'] the person the entry says it honours; fit, optional, one of the genus's own IMR cues the entry says the name refers to; warn, optional, never with fit: a root naming the distinctive feature of other families' IMR cues (a gill-cover spine, barbels, a line or band, bone, blue, yellow, no visible teeth; a body part alone, as fin, tail, lip, tooth or snout, is not one), each [family name, one of its IMR cues verbatim], shown as a warning beside the root (the name study's misleading root). skip: every other genus of circles 1-3 and why it has no line (an etymology unknown or given as a guess, two meanings, a split that is not clear or an old genus name, or a root reading against its own family's IMR cue: rules C1, C2). tools/build_fish.py add_families puts root {p, fit, warn, src} on fish.json genera; learn.js rootLine shows it on the sheet the genus opens. Never an invented etymology.

Neopomacentrus.ety: neo-, new, i.e., a new genus of Pomacentrus

Amblypomacentrus.ety: amblys, blunt, referring to short head of A. breviceps; Pomacentrus

Coradion.ety: kore, pupil of the eye; adion, placed sideways (on the flank)

Centropyge.ety: kentron, thorn or spine; pyge, rump or rear

Pygoplites.ety: pyge, rump or rear; [h]oplites, armed (with a weapon)

Pomacanthus.ety: poma, lid or cover; acanthus, thorn or spine

Genicanthus.ety: genys, cheek; acanthus, thorn or spine

Acanthurus.ety: acanthus, thorn or spine; oura, tail, referring to sharp scalpel-like scales on caudal peduncle (hence the common names surgeonfish and doctorfish)
Acanthurus.fit: One scalpel on the tail base

Hipposcarus.ety: hippos, horse, referring to its “typical horse-like snout”; Scarus

Oxycheilinus.ety: oxy, sharp, i.e., a sharp Cheilinus

Labrichthys.ety: Labrus, similar to and/or closely related to both Labrus and Labroides; ichthys, fish

Hemigymnus.ety: hemi-, partial; gymnos, bare or naked

Pseudocheilinus.ety: pseudo-, false, i.e., although this genus may resemble Cheilinus

Diproctacanthus.ety: di-, two; procto-, anus; acanthus, thorn or spine

Iniistius.ety: inion, back of head; istius, sail

Hologymnosus.ety: holos, whole or entire; gymnosus, bare or naked

Pteragogus.ety: ptera-, fin; agogos, leading, guiding or attracting

Pseudodax.ety: pseudo-, false, i.e., although this genus may resemble Odax

Wetmorella.ety: –ella, diminutive connoting endearment: in honor of ornithologist Alexander Wetmore (1886-1978)

Lutjanus.ety: tautonymous with L. lutjanus, from Ikan (=fish) Lutjang, local Indonesian name for snappers (although Bloch believed it was from Japan)

Scolopsis.ety: scolo-, thorn; opsis, face or appearance

Epinephelus.ety: epinéphelos, ancient Greek for “clouded over,” referring to film or membrane eye of most if not all groupers known to Bloch (although modern accounts mention only a transparent cornea protruding slightly through the orbit)

Diploprion.ety: diplo-, double or two-fold; prion, saw

Pseudanthias.ety: pseudo-, false, i.e., a false Anthias

Ostracion.ety: ancient name for boxfishes, Latinized from the Greek ὀστράκιον, diminutive of óstrakon (ὄστρακον), shell or shellfish

Parupeneus.ety: para-, near, i.e., close to Upeneus but differing in dentition

Mulloidichthys.ety: replacement name for Mulloides Bleeker 1849, preoccupied by Mulloides Richardson 1843 (=Arripis, Arripidae, Scombriformes), originally –oides, having the form of: Mullus, original genus of type species, M. flavolineatus, but differing in dentition; ichthys, fish

Upeneus.ety: misspelling or incorrectly latinized form of hypene, Greek noun for moustache (or by extension beard)

Balistapus.ety: a-, without; pous, foot, i.e., a Balistes without pelvic fins (actually

Rhinecanthus.ety: rhine, rasp; acanthus, thorn or spine

Pseudobalistes.ety: pseudo-, false, originally proposed as a subgenus of Balistes (i.e.

Oxymonacanthus.ety: oxy, sharp, referring to produced snout of O. longirostris, previously placed in Monacanthus

Pseudomonacanthus.ety: pseudo-, false, i.e., not representing the true form of Monacanthus (original genus of type species M. macrurus)

Pervagor.ety: Latin for to wander over or range through
p: to wander over or range through

Paramonacanthus.ety: para-, near, similar to Monacanthus (original genus of P. curtorhynchos) but different in shape of head

Myripristis.ety: myrios (μυρίος), countless or ten-thousand and pristis, saw

Neoniphon.ety: néos (νέος), new, described as “nearly allied” in general form to Niphon (Perciformes: Niphonidae)

Cheilodipterus.ety: cheī́los (χεῖλος), lip, referring to extensible upper lip of C. lineatus; di-, from dýo (δύο), two, and pterus, from pterón (πτερόν) or ptéryx (πτέρυξ), fin

Pristiapogon.ety: pristis, from prístēs (πρίστης), sawyer (but here likely meaning saw), referring to serrated preopercular ridge of P. fraenatus; proposed as a subgenus of Apogon

Foa.ety: from fō, Samoan name for cardinalfishes

Trachinocephalus.ety: Trachino-, referring to resemblance to weever-fishes, Trachinus (Trachinidae); cephalus, from kephalḗ (κεφαλή), head

Aulostomus.ety: aulon, tube; stomus, mouth, referring to small mouth at end of long, compressed tube

Aeoliscus.ety: “moving,” according to the authors, allusion not explained but certainly referring to movable dorsal-fin spine, compared to fixed or rigid dorsal-fin spine of Centriscus

Centriscus.ety: diminutive of kentron, thorn or spine, presumably referring to fixed first spine of anterior dorsal fin (in usual position of caudal fin)

Antennarius.ety: –ius, pertaining to: antenna (i.e., tentacle or feeler), referring to first dorsal-fin spine developed as a small rostral tentacle, which it uses as a “bait” to catch fish

Nudiantennarius.ety: nudus, bare or naked, referring to “naked skin or almost naked skin with only microscopic sized embedded denticles scattered on head and body”; antennarius, an antennariid anglerfish

Abantennarius.ety: ab-, from or away, referring to gill opening “remote from or away from” usual position near base of pectoral fin; antennarius, an antennariid anglerfish

Solenostomus.ety: solen, pipe; stomus, mouth, referring to small mouth at end of long, tube-like snout

Dunckerocampus.ety: Duncker, in honor of ichthyologist Georg Duncker (1870-1953), Zoological Museum Hamburg, who proposed what is now this genus in 1912 but used a preoccupied name (Acanthognathus); kampos, mythological sea monster, probably used here as a general suffix for syngnathids abridged from the seahorse

Trachyrhamphus.ety: trachys, rough; rhamphus, beak, referring to “denticulated

Acentronura.ety: a-, without; kentron, thorn or spine; oura, tail, proposed as a subgenus of Hippocampus without “projections or spikes” (translation) on tail (and body) of A. gracilissima

Doryrhamphus.ety: dory, spear; rhamphus, snout, referring to spines on elongate snout of male D. excisus

Synchiropus.ety: syn-, together; cheiros, hand; opus, foot, referring to membrane connecting pelvic fin to pectoral fin (also present in Callionymus)

Eurypegasus.ety: eury, wide, allusion not explained, probably referring to wider body compared to Pegasus

Scorpaenopsis.ety: opsis, appearance, proposed for S. nesogallica (=gibbosa), similar in appearance to Scorpaena but lacking palatine teeth

Pteroidichthys.ety: –oides, having the form of: Pterois (Pteroinae), close to that genus but distinguished by absence of spines on head (other than edges of opercle and preopercle), among other characters; ichthys, fish

Inimicus.ety: Latin for foe or enemy, “dreaded by fishermen for their stinging spines”

Synanceia.ety: syn-, with; angeíon, cavity, i.e., rutted (“a capite confragola dicta”), referring to large, cavernous heads of S. horrida, S. verrucosa, S. (now Trachicephalus) uranoscopus, S. (now Inimicus) didactylus, and S. (now Scorpaena, in Scorpaenidae) papillosa

Paracentropogon.ety: para-, near, closely related to Centropogon but distinguished (per Bleeker) by the absence of thorn-shaped occipital ridges, by the insertion of the first dorsal spine above the eyes, by very small scales that seem submerged in the skin, and by 12-14 dorsal-fin spines

Dactyloptena.ety: daktylos, finger; ptenos, winged, presumably referring to large, wing-like pectoral fins supported by finger-like rays, similar to the fingers of bat wings

Uranoscopus.ety: urano, sky; scopus, watcher, referring to upwardly directed eyes of U. scaber (and most species of family, hence the common name “stargazer”)

Opistognathus.ety: opisthen, behind; gnathus, jaw, referring to very large upper jaw of O. nigromarginatus, prolonged backward in a long, flexible lamina, reaching to about base of pectoral fin

Ophichthus.ety: ophi-, from óphis (ὄφις), serpent, referring to snake-like appearance of O. ophis; ichthus, variant spelling of ichthýs (ἰχθύς), fish

Brachysomophis.ety: brachýs (βραχύς), short, and sṓma (σῶμα), body, allusion not explained, perhaps referring to moderately elongate body of B. horridus (=crocodilinus) compared with more elongate body of most ophichthines; óphis (ὄφις), serpent, conventional termination for generic names of snake eels, referring to

Callechelys.ety: kállos (κάλλος), beauty, presumably referring to “handsome” (translation) appearance of C. guichenoti (=marmorata); énchelys (ἔγχελυς), eel

Apterichtus.ety: ἀ-, Greek privative, without, and pterón (πτερόν), fin, referring to absence of fins; ichtus, variant spelling of ichthýs (ἰχθύς), fish

Echidna.ety: échidna (ἔχιδνα), viper or adder, allusion not explained, possibly referring to their typical snake-like shape

Gymnothorax.ety: gymnós (γυμνός), bare or naked; thṓrax (θώραξ), breast or chest, referring to absence of pectoral fins

Rhinomuraena.ety: rhinós (ῥινός), genitive of rhís (ῥίς), nose or snout, proposed as a subgenus of Muraena (but treated by Garman as a full genus) with extended anterior nostrils with fan-like extensions at each end

Gymnomuraena.ety: gymnós (γυμνός), bare or naked, referring to absence (or smallness) of dorsal and anal fins; muraena (L.), from mýraina ύραινα), Greek name of Muraena helena and precursor to “moray”

Gorgasia.ety: -ia (L. suffix), pertaining to: the late Gen. William Crawford Gorgas (1854–1920), chief sanitary officer, Panama Canal Zone, through whose department the authors received invaluable aid

Heteroconger.ety: héteros (ἕτερος), different, i.e., a genus that differs from four genera Bleeker believed comprised the conger eels: Conger, Ophiosoma (=Ariosoma), Uroconger and Neoconger (now in Moringuidae)

Triaenodon.ety: triaeno, from tríaina (τρίαινα), trident (having three points); odon, from odoús (ὀδούς), tooth, referring to each having a cusp and two cusplets

Diodon.ety: di-, two; odon, tooth, referring to two fused teeth (but separated by a median suture) in jaws

Cyclichthys.ety: cyclos, round or circular, presumably referring to shape of C. orbicularis when inflated with water or air; ichthys, fish

Trachinotus.ety: trachys, rough; notus, back, referring to five short spines of first dorsal fin of Scomber falcatus Forsskål 1775 (a misidentified T. blochii, not the same species as T. falcatus

Alopias.ety: from alṓpēx (ἀλώπηξ), fox, referring to the ancient vernacular “fox shark,” from its long (and therefore fox-like) tail

Cirrhitichthys.ety: Cirrhitus, similar to that genus but differing in dentition; ichthys, fish

Paracirrhites.ety: para-, near, similar to Cirrhites (alternate spelling of Cirrhitus) but distinguished in having, among other characters, larger and regularly imbricated scales on cheek

Oxycirrhites.ety: oxy, sharp or pointed, referring to very long snout (~½ HL); Cirrhites, alternate spelling of Cirrhitus, type genus of family

Amblycirrhitus.ety: ambly, blunt, allusion not explained, perhaps referring to “abbreviated” head of A. fasciatus (preoccupied by Cirrhitops fasciatus, replaced by A. pinos), and/or its “slightly convex” snout; Cirrhitus, type genus of family

Meiacanthus.ety: meion, less; acanthus, spine, referring to dorsal fin with only 4-8 spines, compared to 10-12 on the related Petroscirtes

Aspidontus.ety: aspis, viper; odon, tooth, referring to dentary canines of prejuvenile A. taeniatus, “surmounted by two long crooked hooks like those of serpents, hiding in the bones of the skull” (translation)

Petroscirtes.ety: petro, stone; scirtes, to leap, referring to Rüppell’s claim that P. mitratus was seen jumping between rocks out of the water hunting for small amphipods; however, since P. mitratus is not amphibious, Rüppell may have confused it with Alticus saliens, observing both blennies at Jubal Island (Egypt

Plagiotremus.ety: plagio-, oblique; trema, hole, referring to “very wide” gape of P. spilistius, with a “lower jaw, which, when closed, shuts obliquely upwards, being capable of retraction even behind the vertical”

Plotosus.ety: from plōtós (πλωτός), swimming or floating, presumably referring to long tail of P. lineatus, confluent with second dorsal and anal fins, which makes it a strong anguilliform swimmer

Priacanthus.ety: prion, saw; acanthus, thorn or spine, referring to serrate preopercular spine of P. macrophthalmus (=hamrur)

Rastrelliger.ety: rastrella, diminutive of rastrum, rake; –iger, to bear, distinguished from Scomber by “excessively long and numerous” gill rakers of R. brachysoma, “longer than eye, the mouth looking as if ‘full of feathers’ ”

Thunnus.ety: from the Greek thynnos, tuna or tunny (replacement name for Thynnus Cuvier 1816, preoccupied by Fabricius 1775 in Hymenoptera)

Heteromycteris.ety: hetero-, different; mycteris, pertaining to the nose, presumably referring to hooked or “sickle-shaped” (translation) snout of H. capensis

Soleichthys.ety: Solea, referring to resemblance to and/or previous placement of S. heterorhinos in that genus; ichthys, fish

Pardachirus.ety: pardos, leopard, probably referring to “numerous brown dots” on eyed side of body, head and fins of P. marmoratus, “with scattered white ocelli edged with brown and with a brown spot in the centre” (i.e., like the spots of a leopard); a-, without and cheiros, hand, referring to lack of pectoral fins

Fistularia.ety: –ia, pertaining to: fistula, pipe, presumably alluding to “Tobacco-pipe Fish,” its common name dating to at least 1685, referring to its shape

Tylosurus.ety: tylos, callus; oura, tail, referring to lateral keels on caudal peduncle

Pictichromis.ety: pictus, painted or colored, referring to bright coloration in life; chromis, common suffix in the family, from Pseudochromis, type genus

Pseudochromis.ety: pseudo-, false, reflecting Rüppell’s belief that this genus is closely related to Chromis (Pomacentridae)

Amblyeleotris.ety: amblýs (ἀμβλύς), blunt, referring to “very obtuse and truncated profile” (translation) of A. periophthalmus, originally placed in Eleotris

Valenciennea.ety: -[i]a (L.), adjectival suffix: eponym not identified but clearly in honor of Achille Valenciennes (1794–1865), co-author of the 22-volume Histoire Naturelle des Poissons (1828–1850), a basic reference for Bleeker and other ichthyologists of the time

Asterropteryx.ety: a-, privative, i.e., not; sterrós (στερρός), firm or stiff; ptéryx (πτέρυξ), fin, referring to slender and flexible dorsal-fin spines of A. semipunctata

Lubricogobius.ety: lubricus (L.), slippery, presumably referring to absence of scales; gobius (L.), a fish of small value or a gudgeon, i.e., a goby

Amblygobius.ety: amblýs (ἀμβλύς), blunt, referring to compressed, convex and blunt head of A. sphynx; gobius (L.), a fish of small value or a gudgeon, i.e., a goby

Trimma.ety: trimma (τρίμμα), anything rubbed or crushed, allusion not explained, perhaps referring to “firmer” texture and/or “less translucent” color compared with the similar Eviota

Hazeus.ety: Latinization of haze, Japanese name for a small goby
p: Japanese name for a small goby

Vanderhorstia.ety: -ia (L. suffix), belonging to: Cornelius Jan van der Horst (1889–1951), Head of the Zoology Department, Witwatserand University (Johannesburg, South Africa), “well known as a marine biologist”

Gnatholepis.ety: gnáthos (γνάθος), jaw; lepís (λεπίς), scale, allusion not explained, presumably referring to scales on head and cheek of G. anjerensis

Koumansetta.ety: -etta (L.), diminutive connoting endearment: in honor of goby taxonomist Frederik Petrus Koumans (1905–1977), Rijksmuseum van Natuurlijke Historie (Leiden, Netherlands), who prepared a description of K. rainfordi when he visited the Australian Museum in 1938 but did not name it at the time; since

Eviota.ety: ev-, Latinization (for euphony) of eū́- (εὖ), an intensive prefix, e.g., good, well or very; iota (ι), ninth and smallest letter of the Greek alphabet, often figuratively used to describe anything small or insignificant, referring to E. epiphanes, which, at 1.0–1.9 cm in length, Jenkins claimed was
p: ninth and smallest letter of the Greek alphabet

Ctenogobiops.ety: ṓps (ὦψ), eye or face (i.e., appearance), “[c]losely related” (and presumably similar) to Ctenogobius (Oxudercidae)

Stonogobiops.ety: stonyx (στονυ), any sharp point, referring to large vomerine teeth of S. dracula; gobius (L.), goby, and ṓps (ὦψ), eye or face (i.e., appearance)

Paragobiodon.ety: pará (παρά), near, presumably referring to similarity to and/or close relationship with Gobiodon

Mahidolia.ety: -ia (L. suffix), belonging to: the late Mahidol Adulyadej (1892–1929), Prince of Songkla, for his “substantial” interest in the fishes and fisheries of Siam (Thailand)

Tomiyamichthys.ety: in honor of ichthyologist Itiro (sometimes spelled Ichiro) Tomiyama (1906-1981), Tokyo Imperial University, who described type species, T. oni, in 1936; ichthýs (ἰχθύς), fish

Gobiodon.ety: gobius (L.), a fish of small value or a gudgeon, i.e., a goby; odon, from odoús (ὀδούς), tooth, referring to pair of posterior canines near symphysis of lower jaw of G. heterospilos

Grammistes.ety: lined, referring to six (maximum) white-to-yellow horizontal lines on body of G. orientalis (=sexlineatus)
warn: Often a horizontal line along the body

Ostorhinchus.ety: osteo-, from ostéon (ὀστέον), bone; rhynchus, from rhýnchos (ῥύγχος), snout, referring to bony jaws of O. fleurieu, very much advanced and jagged, taking the place of teeth
warn: Bony carapace: square, triangular or rounded

Caesio.ety: from caesius, blue, referring to upper body of C. caerulaurea, described as a “sky blue most pleasant to the eye” (translation)

Pomacentrus.ety: poma, lid or cover; kentron, thorn or spine, referring to serrations and prickles along margins of opercular bones of P. pavo
warn: Spine on the gill cover (opercular spine)

Plectropomus.ety: plectrum, spur; pomus, lid or covering, referring to ventral edge of preopercle with three large downward-projecting spines (often covered by skin)
warn: Spine on the gill cover (opercular spine)

Pogonoperca.ety: pogon, beard, referring to barbel on lower jaw of P. ocellata; perca, a perch-like fish
warn: Two barbels to search the sand for food

Taenianotus.ety: taenia, narrow flat band; notus, back, referring to long dorsal fin, extending from head to tail
warn: Black band over the eye in adults

Taeniura.ety: taenia (L.), from tainía (ταινία), band or ribbon;ourá (οὐρά), tail, referring to fin fold underneath tail of T. lymna
warn: Black band over the eye in adults

Flavocaranx.ety: flavus, yellow, referring to yellowish body color; Caranx, type genus of family
warn: Yellow on the body and a yellow saddle

Gnathanodon.ety: gnathus, jaw; an-, without; odon, teeth, referring to absence of teeth on jaws (and vomer and tongue, on specimens >90 mm)
